She swims recreationally, keeps a robotics testing notebook, and weighs whether another competitive season deserves the time. Her health is usually well managed, and she wants future study to allow sleep, friendship, and dependable supplies.

ambitions: Wants education beyond high school
Imagines regular workdays, a good pool, and enough flexibility for people she loves.

biography.selfDescription: I like knowing whether something improved and why. Diabetes takes planning, but sometimes the harder thing is convincing people that I can decide when I need help and when I just want to swim.
openQuestions: Would she enjoy testing outside a noisy club?
Is reduced competition a lasting preference?

biography.name: Priya Ramaswamy

background.family: Lives with parents, grandmother, and younger brother; they share chores and lively movie arguments.
background.finances: Upper-middle income from engineering and school administration; parents support college and expect thoughtful spending.
background.geography: Plano, Texas, with relatives in Chennai and New Jersey.
background.cultureLanguages: English most often; understands Tamil better than she speaks it, with patient encouragement from grandmother.
background.school: Large public high school with advanced courses and orchestra.
background.accessOpportunities: Tutoring and summer programs are accessible; she increasingly chooses nearby informal activities.

timeline.story: Priya made tiny blankets for dolls with her grandmother. She liked choosing scraps and telling long stories about the dolls, while refusing to let anyone describe her unusual color combinations as a mistake.

Her parents enrolled her in violin and a math circle. She enjoyed puzzles with one friend, but group music stayed memorable because several people could make something none could produce alone in their bedrooms.

A cousin taught her bowling, and she began requesting the alley for birthdays. Tracking small changes in her approach became a private interest that surprised relatives who associated her almost entirely with school assignments.

During remote school she recorded spoken family recipes. Full transcription became tedious, so Priya switched to photographs and short audio clips, then discovered that younger cousins actually used this less formal collection.

She entered middle-school orchestra assuming violin would remain central, but enjoyed organizing rehearsal snacks and sharing music recommendations more than practicing difficult passages. She stayed in the ensemble while admitting that difference to her teacher.

Priya joined a bowling league and repaired thrifted clothes with a friend. She declined an additional academic camp because she wanted one summer of repeated local friendships, rather than another impressive but brief introduction.

She takes demanding classes, bowls weekly, and builds a small recipe site using a beginner tool. Many subjects excite her, but she resists letting the most impressive option become her default before understanding its everyday demands. She recently taught her brother a simple repair and discovered that waiting through his mistakes required more patience than doing it herself.

ambitions: Wants to experience a college campus
Imagines an adult household with shared meals and several hobbies, even if her work stays uncertain.

biography.selfDescription: I'm good at school, but that doesn't mean every school thing is what I care about most. Sometimes the best part of my week is figuring out why one bowling ball suddenly did what I wanted.
openQuestions: Will site maintenance remain enjoyable?
Which interests persist without comparison or recognition?

biography.name: Evan Markham

background.family: Lives with parents and an older sister; family members are close and have learned to ask before offering reassurance.
background.finances: Comfortable middle income; counseling is covered by insurance and parents can help with college expenses.
background.geography: Round Rock, Texas, in a quiet subdivision with nearby trails.
background.cultureLanguages: White, English-speaking family; grandparents live in Oklahoma and visits involve board games and elaborate breakfasts.
background.school: Public high school; fictional generalized anxiety disorder diagnosed at thirteen, with counseling and flexible presentation arrangements.
background.accessOpportunities: Has reliable technology and supportive teachers; he sometimes declines opportunities despite their availability.

timeline.story: Evan loved helping set the breakfast table at his grandparents’ house and wanted to know exactly who would sit where. He also invented absurd games that made the same orderly adults laugh until they cried.

He became fascinated by pond insects after a field trip and kept sketches in a notebook. Before outings he asked repeated questions about toilets and pickup times, but usually relaxed once the group arrived.

A teacher let him lead a short nature walk for classmates. He practiced every sentence and enjoyed their questions, although he spent the previous evening imagining that he would forget the route or misidentify everything.

Remote classes reduced some social pressure but gave his worries more room. He checked submissions repeatedly, sometimes missing family movie night despite having finished the actual assignment an hour before the deadline.

At thirteen, counseling helped him recognize generalized anxiety and practice completing manageable tasks without endless checking. His family stopped promising that nothing could go wrong and instead helped him plan how to handle ordinary mistakes.

He joined a bird count with a familiar adult, then returned with a friend. Evan still rehearsed introductions, but found that attention to distant calls occasionally interrupted his attention to what other people might think.

He now records neighborhood birds, plays strategic games, and occasionally presents short observations in class. Symptoms vary with workload; he is considering campus size and counseling continuity while wanting future choices to reflect curiosity as well as comfort. Last month he submitted one assignment without a final reread, then went birding before learning the grade.

ambitions: Wants to try studying beyond home
Imagines a calm household with outdoor time and dependable friendships.

biography.selfDescription: I can be excited and scared about the same afternoon. I'm getting better at going anyway, especially when there is something outside to pay attention to instead of just my own thoughts.
openQuestions: Does a small campus appeal independently of anxiety?
Would he enjoy presenting when preparation time is limited?

biography.name: Rhett Calder

background.family: Lives with parents and two sisters on a family cattle operation; extended relatives share some seasonal work.
background.finances: Land and equipment provide substantial assets, while annual income fluctuates; education savings are available.
background.geography: Outside Abilene, Texas, forty minutes from school.
background.cultureLanguages: White, English-speaking family with rural Texas roots; attends a local church and also questions family assumptions openly.
background.school: Small public high school with agricultural classes and limited arts electives.
background.accessOpportunities: Has machinery experience and family connections but few nearby formal arts spaces; Texas colleges and technical schools are reachable by planned visits.

timeline.story: Rhett followed his older sister around the yard and invented names for clouds while adults repaired fences. He liked the animals but preferred listening to his grandmother’s stories over watching televised rodeo with cousins.

He learned simple animal-care routines, including checking water tubs before school. A patient teacher encouraged his detailed retellings of family events, and he began drawing speech bubbles in the margins of homework.

A visiting puppeteer performed at the library, and Rhett spent weeks making a cardboard stage. His father helped cut openings, then attended several long performances whose plots changed whenever the family dog wandered through.

During remote schooling he had more ranch chores but also recorded little radio dramas with his sisters. Editing out wind noise frustrated him until he moved the microphone into a closet filled with coats.

He tried football because most friends played and liked the collective routines more than contact. After a season he moved to assisting with announcements, learning to pronounce unfamiliar names before speaking them publicly.

A school essay about an unremarkable stock-tank repair received praise for dialogue. Rhett joined an online youth writing group, where feedback from strangers challenged both his descriptions of rural life and his assumptions about theirs.

He helps with chores, writes short audio scenes, and reads scripts through the library. He knows ranch work can be satisfying and tiring in the same day; he wants broader experience before deciding how close to the family operation to remain. His younger sister now asks to record one character’s voice, introducing a collaboration he cannot control completely.

avoids: Being assumed to love contact sports
ambitions: Wants education with room for writing
Imagines returning often to family while having a home whose routines he chooses.

biography.selfDescription: People hear where I live and think they know my whole personality. I like parts of the ranch a lot, and I also like spending three hours fixing one line of dialogue.
openQuestions: Would he enjoy live performance?
How much distance would feel expansive rather than isolating?

biography.name: Rojin Baran

background.family: Lives with parents and a younger cousin whose parents work overseas; adults share responsibility and make space for private time.
background.finances: Parents’ restaurant and bookkeeping earnings cover essentials; educational travel requires saving.
background.geography: Arlington, Texas, after moving from the Midwest at eight.
background.cultureLanguages: Kurdish American household using Kurmanji and English; family stories include several different migrations without a single agreed interpretation.
background.school: Public high school with an early-college partnership; takes one supported dual-credit class.
background.accessOpportunities: Library workshops, community tennis courts, and nearby college visits are accessible; household work limits some weekends.

timeline.story: Rojin loved rearranging cushions into forts and recording pretend weather forecasts on a parent’s phone. Adults laughed at her dramatic warnings, and she learned to repeat the same scene differently for different relatives.

She helped count napkins at the restaurant and became interested in how many could fit in different boxes. At home, her cousin taught her card tricks that depended on remembering what people had already seen.

After the move to Texas, a neighbor invited her to tennis. She liked the quick adjustments and having a clearly bounded court, even though the scoring system initially seemed stranger than any school math lesson.

She stopped organized lessons during remote school but practiced against a wall. Recording short clips helped her see why some strokes failed; she began enjoying replay and explanation as much as winning points.

Rojin used she and they pronouns with friends and later discussed them at home. Reactions included questions and awkward mistakes, but continued family affection made room for conversation without requiring every relative to understand immediately.

She helped prepare multilingual restaurant notices and learned that literal translation did not always answer customers’ questions. A dual-credit writing class introduced longer research assignments, and she discovered that organizing evidence could feel surprisingly absorbing.

Rojin plays community tennis, helps with restaurant inventory, and is testing whether she likes research beyond familiar subjects. She wants more choice in her schedule and is comparing local college routes without treating staying nearby as failure or leaving as proof of success.

ambitions: Interested in further study without a settled subject
Imagines an adult life with a welcoming home, regular exercise, and family within visiting distance.

biography.selfDescription: I like seeing a replay because what felt obvious can look completely different. I don't think choosing a future should depend on proving that I'm either exactly like my family or completely unlike them.
openQuestions: Will research appeal outside self-chosen topics?
How much family work would she choose if transportation were easier?

biography.name: Bethany Kline

background.family: Lives with parents, three younger siblings, and a dog; the household is affectionate, busy, and regularly hosts neighborhood children.
background.finances: Middle income from electrical work and part-time tutoring; family budgets carefully for co-op fees.
background.geography: Outside Waco, Texas, with weekly trips into the city.
background.cultureLanguages: White evangelical Christian family; English at home, with discussion of differing beliefs encouraged within respectful conversation.
background.school: Homeschooled through a parent-led plan and co-op science and literature classes; documented coursework supports later college applications.
background.accessOpportunities: Community theater, a public library, and local college events widen an otherwise small peer network.

timeline.story: Bethany narrated stories while stacking blocks, insisting that every tower contained a different family. Her mother wrote down one long story, and Bethany liked hearing her own invented words read back at bedtime.

Early lessons happened around younger siblings’ naps. She learned quickly when reading alone but became frustrated when interrupted, so her father built a simple folding screen she could place around a work table.

A co-op science activity involved constructing paper bridges. Bethany disliked the first collapse, then spent an entire afternoon changing folds and recording how many coins each bridge held before asking anyone to admire it.

When community events paused, she wrote letters to an older church member and learned that a good question could bring a much longer answer. Her poems gradually included details from other people’s ordinary routines.

She joined community theater as a small-role performer and found rehearsals more socially complicated than expected. Missing a cue upset her, but returning the next evening helped her discover that mistakes rarely remained the main story.

A co-op debate about water use led her to read municipal documents and ask an engineer questions after a public event. She liked the technical explanation while remaining unsure whether she would enjoy long days of similar calculations.

Bethany studies algebra, writes poems, and helps younger students build bridges at co-op. She is considering dual enrollment and wants sustained contact with people whose views differ from hers, while keeping relationships in her existing community. She recently asked to attend a campus open lecture on her own, with a parent collecting her afterward.

motivations: Understanding how people and systems fit together
ambitions: Considering dual enrollment
Imagines a home open to friends and enough quiet time to read and make things.
struggles: Sometimes treats a mistake as a verdict

biography.selfDescription: I like a problem that gives me something concrete to try, and I also like poems that don't resolve everything. I want to hear more viewpoints without pretending the people who raised me don't matter.
openQuestions: Does she prefer technical design or the process of trying alternatives?
How will a larger classroom affect her participation?

biography.name: Caleb Hensley

background.family: Lives with mother and maternal grandfather; his father has been incarcerated since Caleb was twelve and they exchange letters.
background.finances: Grandfather’s pension and mother’s warehouse wages cover a modest rental; little money remains for extracurricular fees.
background.geography: Texarkana, Texas, after earlier years in eastern Kentucky.
background.cultureLanguages: White, English-speaking family with Appalachian roots; music and practical jokes remain important parts of family contact.
background.school: Public high school; attendance is consistent now after a difficult transition year.
background.accessOpportunities: School equipment, a youth music room, and nearby college or trade-program visits are available when work schedules allow.

timeline.story: Caleb liked sitting beside his father while he played guitar, copying the rhythm on an upside-down bucket. He also watched his mother sew curtains and repeatedly asked why one side of the cloth looked different.

He learned basic chords and sang loudly with cousins. His teacher described him as talkative during group work, but he also spent long stretches quietly arranging toy vehicles into elaborate parking lots with working entrances.

The family moved for work, and Caleb missed familiar relatives more than expected. A school custodian showed him where the music room was, and having one recognizable adult made the larger building less intimidating.

During remote lessons he helped his grandfather scan old photographs and identify people. He began asking questions about family stories that adults usually told as jokes, noticing how different versions left out different details.

His father’s incarceration changed household finances and made some classmates’ questions painful. Caleb argued more at school until a counselor helped him practice responses that protected privacy without requiring him to deny their relationship.

He started paid grocery shifts and borrowed a school guitar. Playing with two friends gave him a reliable weekly commitment; when one quit, Caleb learned to keep meeting without turning the absence into another personal rejection.

He balances school, work, and helping his grandfather with online forms. He wants education after graduation but worries about leaving his mother with more responsibilities; music remains important even when he cannot explain what place it should occupy later.

motivations: Contributing without losing his own future
ambitions: Wants postsecondary options to remain open
Imagines a dependable home with music and people who do not need him to explain everything.

biography.selfDescription: I don't want every fact about me to turn into a story about my dad. I like making things sound right together, and I'm still figuring out how school, work, and my family can fit together too.
openQuestions: Would he want to leave if household support increased?
Does formal music study appeal or would it change what he values about playing?

biography.name: Darius Bellamy

background.family: Lives with his mother, stepfather, and younger sister; adults coordinate calendars without treating every forgotten item as a moral failure.
background.finances: Middle income from transit operations and dental-office work; some college savings, with cost still important.
background.geography: Dallas, Texas, near a bus route and a busy neighborhood park.
background.cultureLanguages: Black American, English-speaking family; music, cookouts, and an extended cousin network shape weekends.
background.school: Public high school; fictional ADHD identified at ten, managed with chosen medication, coaching, movement breaks, and written task prompts.
background.accessOpportunities: Has school media equipment and a recreation center; support makes demanding activities possible, although coordination takes effort.

timeline.story: Darius built long obstacle courses from cushions, then persuaded adults to time him. He loved inventing rules but forgot the previous version so often that his mother began drawing little diagrams for everyone to follow.

He enjoyed classroom demonstrations and interrupted with questions before teachers finished explaining. At home he could spend an hour arranging recorded sound effects, while a ten-minute worksheet seemed to stretch through the entire evening.

He joined a neighborhood soccer team and liked tracking opponents’ movements. His coach noticed that a short instruction immediately before practice worked better than a long list given while everyone stood around waiting.

An ADHD evaluation helped the family understand uneven attention and task initiation. Darius tried supports with his clinician and teachers, learning that a written next step could matter as much as simply being interested.

He made short videos of park games with friends, then learned that editing required patient file management. After losing footage once, he created a naming routine and asked a friend to check the final folder.

A media teacher invited him to record sound for school interviews. He enjoyed getting clean audio and putting nervous speakers at ease, but underestimated editing time until missed homework forced a more realistic weekly calendar.

He now combines soccer, occasional video work, and a few paid weekend setup jobs. His systems work best when adults coordinate rather than duplicate reminders; he wants further training but is still learning which environments let him stay engaged sustainably.

ambitions: Wants training with practical projects
Imagines varied days, regular games with friends, and an apartment he can keep manageable.

biography.selfDescription: I can care about something and still lose track of the boring step that makes it work. When I have a system I actually use, I can do much more than people expect from seeing my backpack.
openQuestions: Which planning supports will transfer to a new setting?
Would routine production work hold the appeal of occasional school projects?

biography.name: Taylor

background.family: Lives with parents and a younger brother.
background.finances: Moderate income; family prioritizes outdoor access over expensive outings.
background.geography: Boerne, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home; frequent family hikes with local friends.
background.school: Public high school with a supervised water-monitoring club.
background.accessOpportunities: Field equipment through school and shared data sheets; no hazardous independent fieldwork.

timeline.story: In 2014, Taylor liked walking beside shallow creeks with an adult and watching leaves move around stones. They also enjoyed noisy group games, though they sometimes wandered back to inspect a puddle after the game ended.

At six, they began drawing routes from family walks. During 2017, a dry section of creek surprised them, and they asked relatives whether the water had moved somewhere else or simply disappeared into the ground.

In 2018, Taylor kept an informal weather notebook and discovered that memory alone exaggerated how often rain spoiled weekend plans. They liked comparing the notes with family recollections, including their own confident but inaccurate statements.

During 2020, local walks became a regular household activity. Taylor returned to the same places and noticed changes after rain, while school assignments felt more interesting when connected with something they could observe outdoors.

At twelve, Taylor joined supervised water monitoring and learned to record location and conditions. In 2023, they entered results into a shared sheet and repeated a measurement when it differed sharply from the readings around it.

Across 2024 and 2025, Taylor continued field notes and learned that uncertainty did not always disappear after another measurement. Treating patients and managing a shop sounded unappealing; returning to the stream to investigate a change still sounded worthwhile.

At sixteen in 2026, Taylor is exploring Texas science programs and asking about introductory field courses. They imagine a simple life with hiking equipment and modest expenses, while knowing that club sampling does not prepare them for hazardous sites or independent scientific responsibility.

ambitions: Explore science study with field components
They imagine a simple home near walking routes with time and basic equipment for outdoor exploration.

biography.selfDescription: I like going back to the same place and finding it is not really the same. Sometimes another measurement makes the question clearer instead of answering it, and that can be interesting rather than disappointing.
openQuestions: Will laboratory analysis appeal as much as field notes?
How would unpleasant weather and repetitive sampling affect motivation?

biography.name: Cameron

background.family: Lives with parents and a nearby uncle who shares workshop time.
background.finances: Moderate income; technical study would require cost comparison.
background.geography: Tyler, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English; family often exchanges practical help with neighbors.
background.school: Public high school with basic science and technical electives.
background.accessOpportunities: Bicycle work with an experienced relative and observation of engine maintenance.

timeline.story: In 2014, Cameron liked toy vehicles but also spent long afternoons making paper masks with cousins. Their favorite games involved something breaking in an imaginary journey and a character figuring out how everyone could continue.

At six, they learned basic bicycle care with an uncle. During 2017, they were impatient to replace a squeaky part, and the uncle showed how checking alignment first could avoid replacing something that was not actually broken.

In 2018, Cameron joined a recreation-center group and liked helping set up equipment. They enjoyed explaining a simple adjustment to another child more than selling raffle tickets, even when the sale supported an activity they liked.

During 2020, they used extra home time to clean a bicycle and keep notes with adult guidance. A repair that seemed successful failed its first check, making the final testing feel more important than the satisfying moment of reassembly.

At twelve, Cameron began logging bicycle repairs in a notebook. In 2023, they watched an experienced relative maintain an engine, asking what each check ruled out while leaving unfamiliar or potentially dangerous tasks to the adult.

Across 2024 and 2025, they continued supervised bicycle work and became curious about larger machines. Workshop routines and clear explanations to users sounded appealing, while prolonged desk research and sales conversations remained much less attractive.

At sixteen in 2026, Cameron is comparing Texas technical training in vehicle repair and industrial machinery. They want to see both settings before choosing, knowing informal repairs do not establish professional competence or reveal how daily workplace demands would feel.

ambitions: Compare vehicle and machinery training
They imagine a practical independent home with reliable transport, a small workspace, and time with friends.

biography.selfDescription: I want to know why something stopped working before I start changing parts. I enjoy the workshop, but I have only seen a small part of what repair work can involve, and I want to compare the real settings.
openQuestions: How much written technical material would they accept for a meaningful repair?
Which workplace routines appeal after direct observation?

biography.name: Finley

background.family: Lives with his mother and stepfather; younger cousins visit frequently.
background.finances: Stable moderate income; college study would involve budgeting.
background.geography: Frisco, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home; family enjoys reading aloud and board games.
background.school: Public high school with a supervised homework club.
background.accessOpportunities: Peer-support opportunities and teacher feedback; no professional classroom role.

timeline.story: In 2014, Finley enjoyed showing cousins how to play a simple game, then became frustrated when they wanted to invent their own version. He also liked picture books about animals and building towers that rarely survived the afternoon.

At six, he began reading familiar instructions aloud to another child. During 2017, a teacher reminded him that explaining more loudly was not the same as explaining differently, a distinction he understood gradually rather than all at once.

In 2018, Finley liked both science and language lessons, especially when an example made a difficult idea suddenly understandable. He sometimes completed a friend’s task to help, only to discover that the friend remained just as confused afterward.

During 2020, he helped a younger cousin with schoolwork over video. He learned to ask what the cousin thought the question meant, which often revealed a different problem from the one Finley had initially prepared to explain.

At twelve, Finley joined a supervised homework club. In 2023, he tried two explanations for the same mathematics idea and found it more satisfying when the pupil could continue independently than when Finley simply supplied the answer.

Across 2024 and 2025, he continued supporting younger pupils and receiving teacher guidance. He enjoyed noticing where understanding stopped, while recognizing that a small homework group did not show him the demands of managing a full classroom.

At sixteen in 2026, Finley is exploring Texas education programs and introductory observation opportunities. He wants a steady life with time for friends rather than a very high income, and remains unsure how professional teaching would compare with the specific tutoring moments he likes.

avoids: Doing a pupil’s work for them
ambitions: Explore education study and broader observation
He imagines a dependable routine with friends nearby and time outside work for ordinary interests.

biography.selfDescription: I like the moment somebody can take the next step without me. Helping with homework has made me curious about teaching, but I have not been responsible for a room full of pupils who all need different things at once.
openQuestions: How would whole-class demands change his enjoyment?
Which ages and subjects interest him after wider observation?

biography.name: Quinn

background.family: Lives with parents; an uncle runs a small family delivery business.
background.finances: Moderate income; transport costs receive careful attention.
background.geography: Laredo, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English and Spanish within family.
background.school: Public high school with school-event volunteer opportunities.
background.accessOpportunities: Family planning conversations and adult-guided address checks; no commercial driving.

timeline.story: In 2014, Quinn liked arranging toy vehicles into routes across the floor and then changing the destinations. They also enjoyed drawing animals, with no particular interest in making the pictures look realistic or showing them to a group.

At six, they began asking how long familiar trips should take. During 2017, an adult helped them understand that distance alone did not determine time, especially when stops, traffic, and waiting were part of the journey.

In 2018, Quinn visited an uncle’s family delivery business and noticed the planning behind departures. They liked checking which items belonged together, but did not drive or take on work beyond simple age-appropriate assistance.

During 2020, they helped family compare routes for ordinary errands and learned that an apparently efficient plan could fail if a destination was closed. They liked revising a map more than arguing about whose first suggestion had been best.

At twelve, Quinn helped arrange a school delivery schedule with adult oversight. In 2023, they checked addresses carefully and learned to ask when an abbreviation could refer to more than one street or building.

Across 2024 and 2025, Quinn continued noticing timing and destination details in family conversations. Paid training and independent work sounded attractive, but commercial vehicles, lifting demands, and overnight work remained outside anything they had tried.

At sixteen in 2026, Quinn is exploring Texas transport-related training information while comparing hours, licensing, and costs. They like the idea of movement and independence, without yet knowing whether daily driving conditions or particular schedules would suit them.

ambitions: Compare paid training and actual work schedules
They imagine modest independent living with reliable transport, savings, and enough time to stay connected to family.

biography.selfDescription: I like seeing how the stops fit together before anyone leaves. The independent part sounds appealing, but I have not driven commercially or worked overnight, so I do not want to confuse an interesting map with knowing the whole job.
openQuestions: Which schedules feel acceptable after direct observation?
How do real transport costs alter the attraction of independence?

biography.name: Charlie

background.family: Lives with parents and a younger sister.
background.finances: Moderate stable income; future lifestyle has not been worked out.
background.geography: Austin, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English; family encourages trying available community activities.
background.school: Public high school with several short classroom and after-school introductions.
background.accessOpportunities: Brief participation in multiple activities; some guidance helps across unfamiliar tasks.

timeline.story: In 2014, Charlie happily joined whatever game was underway and often wanted to try a second one before the first ended. He enjoyed building, pretend stories, and outdoor play without any lasting favorite emerging from the mix.

At six, he liked new classroom activities and asked to try materials other children were using. During 2017, adults noticed his enthusiasm but could not identify a particular skill or subject that consistently stood apart.

In 2018, Charlie took part briefly in several school activities, enjoying being included and hearing new ideas. He sometimes needed help with instructions, and the activity that sounded most exciting often depended on what friends had mentioned that morning.

During 2020, he tried ordinary school projects at home and liked the prospect of many different tasks. Some remained unfinished once the novelty passed, but there was no sustained specialist project from which to infer a particular direction.

At twelve, Charlie continued saying that most new options sounded interesting. In 2023, he joined short school activities involving helping, making, and presenting, without enough repeated experience to establish which kinds of everyday work he preferred.

Across 2024 and 2025, he considered several creative possibilities and liked all the examples shown to him. That broad enthusiasm did not mean he had distinct evidence for each occupation, and he still found guidance useful when moving beyond an introduction.

At sixteen in 2026, Charlie is exploring Texas college, practical training, and several working settings. His lifestyle picture is similarly tentative, and he wants opportunities to repeat activities long enough to discover differences that first impressions have not yet revealed.

avoids: Few settled dislikes; this may change with experience
activities: Brief participation in several school activities
demonstratedSkills: Participates with some guidance; no specialist mastery is assumed
ambitions: Repeat several experiences before narrowing options
He imagines several possible adult lifestyles and has not settled on location, spending, or routine.

biography.selfDescription: Most things sound interesting when somebody first explains them. I probably need to do some of them more than once before I know which parts I like, and I do not want every enthusiastic yes to become a permanent plan.
openQuestions: Which interests persist through repetition and frustration?
What preferences emerge when time prevents trying everything?

biography.name: Priya Desai

background.family: Lives with parents and an older sister who attends college nearby.
background.finances: High household income; parents fund lessons and travel.
background.geography: Plano, Texas, with frequent Dallas visits.
background.cultureLanguages: Gujarati and English at home; participates selectively in family religious events.
background.school: Competitive private school with extensive laboratory and arts facilities.
background.accessOpportunities: Tutors, transportation, and campus contacts are readily available.

timeline.story: In 2014, Priya liked mixing spices with her grandmother and naming the smells. She resisted formal piano practice, then voluntarily spent an hour figuring out melodies from television when nobody corrected her posture.

At six, she entered a well-equipped school where adults praised her neat work. In 2017, she started hiding unfinished drawings after a classmate laughed at a horse, though she continued sketching animals privately.

In 2018, a family road trip included several museums. Priya remembered the exhibit benches and visitor traffic as much as the objects, then rearranged her bedroom to make a better route around the furniture.

During 2020, she had uninterrupted online lessons and space to work alone. She nevertheless missed noisy group projects and spent evenings building a collaborative fictional town in a game with friends from two schools.

At twelve, she asked to stop piano examinations and keep casual lessons. In 2023, she joined a robotics group but gravitated toward interviewing potential users rather than competing to write the most complex code.

In 2024, Priya helped a neighborhood library test signs for a children’s event. Several visitors misunderstood her first design. She revised it after watching them, feeling embarrassed at first and then unexpectedly proud of the improvement.

At sixteen in 2026, she takes demanding science courses, sketches public spaces, and sometimes wishes her schedule contained nothing impressive. She is comparing Texas campus visits partly by whether students seem able to change their minds.

avoids: Adults introducing her as the successful sister
ambitions: Try an unscheduled summer month
Find interdisciplinary courses
She imagines an adult life with autonomy over her schedule, close relationships, and chances to keep trying unfamiliar subjects.
struggles: Treats ordinary mistakes as public events

biography.selfDescription: I have access to a lot, and sometimes I use that as a reason I should already know what I want. I like science, but I also notice how people move around a room before I notice the equipment.
openQuestions: Which activities would remain without external praise?
How much structure does she actually want?

biography.name: Devin Laurent

background.family: Lives with his mother and stepmother; an adult half-sister visits frequently.
background.finances: Low-to-moderate income with dependable rent and essentials.
background.geography: Apartment complex in Baton Rouge, Louisiana; relatives in Beaumont, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English; family preserves some Louisiana Creole recipes and expressions.
background.school: Public high school with a strong culinary elective and limited advanced sciences.
background.accessOpportunities: Community center and relatives can support occasional Texas campus trips.

timeline.story: In 2014, Devin spent time in his grandmother’s kitchen and disliked sticky dough on his hands. He preferred arranging the serving table, counting chairs, and deciding where everyone could sit without blocking the doorway.
At six, he joined a recreation-center chess group. In 2017, he lost many games to an older neighbor but returned because reviewing the game afterward felt like solving a puzzle with another person.

In 2018, Devin began weekend visits to cousins in Beaumont. Their crowded, cheerful house made him curious about different routines, and he started keeping a notebook comparing bus routes and public playgrounds between the cities.

During 2020, he shared a laptop with his mother and learned to plan work around her evening classes. He cooked simple meals despite still disliking some textures, using utensils and gloves when they helped.

At twelve, Devin tried basketball and decided he preferred keeping score to playing. By 2023, he was helping a community-center coach settle scheduling disagreements and discovering that adults sometimes needed the same reminders as children.

In 2024, a culinary elective made him interested in safe food storage and scaling recipes. In 2025, he volunteered for event setup, enjoying the planning while sometimes finding the constant conversation afterward unexpectedly tiring.

At sixteen in 2026, Devin is comparing Louisiana options with Texas programs near family in Beaumont. He likes the idea of college but is equally interested in whether a short credential would give him something tangible to build on.

ambitions: Explore study near extended family
Earn a useful first qualification
He imagines a dependable home near relatives, a few close friendships, and a daily rhythm with both busy collaboration and quiet hours.

biography.selfDescription: I enjoy making a gathering happen, and I might still leave early once it is happening. I do not have one big plan; I want to try something long enough to know whether I like the everyday parts.
openQuestions: Would event planning remain enjoyable under deadline pressure?
Is Texas appealing because of programs or because cousins are there?

biography.name: Rafael Yazzie

background.family: Lives with his mother and stepfather; extended family lives in northern Arizona.
background.finances: Steady moderate income from healthcare and municipal work.
background.geography: Flagstaff, Arizona; stepfather’s family lives near San Marcos, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Diné and English family connections; Rafael understands some Diné phrases and asks relatives when unsure.
background.school: Public high school with outdoor and media electives.
background.accessOpportunities: Local outdoor access, school media equipment, and Texas family visits.

timeline.story: In 2014, Rafael enjoyed listening to relatives tell stories during visits and insisted on drawing the vehicles mentioned in them. He also liked helping wash dishes because adults sometimes continued interesting conversations around the sink.

At six, he learned to skate at a recreation center and fell often without much embarrassment. During 2017, he began making sound effects for the short videos he and a cousin recorded on a borrowed phone.

In 2018, Rafael joined a school garden and wanted to understand why the same seedlings grew differently in two beds. His first explanation was wrong, and he enjoyed asking a volunteer to help test another possibility.

During 2020, he spent more time outdoors with his household and recorded small sounds from ordinary walks. He disliked online group assignments but maintained friendships through swapping short audio clips and increasingly elaborate guesses about their sources.

At twelve, Rafael started editing school announcements. In 2023, a family trip to Texas made him curious about rivers and hot-weather cities, though he disliked the traffic and missed being able to walk into nearby open space.

Across 2024 and 2025, he helped document a neighborhood stream project and tried indoor climbing. He liked interviewing volunteers, but found that turning hours of recordings into a short final piece required more patience than collecting them.

At sixteen in 2026, Rafael is looking at a Texas summer environmental-media workshop near relatives and a local outdoor course. He feels no need to decide whether his future should center on landscapes, storytelling, or something he has not yet tried.

avoids: Uncredited use of other people’s stories
ambitions: Try a workshop in a different landscape
He imagines an adult life with outdoor access, time to visit relatives, and friends who enjoy making things together.
struggles: Sometimes collects more material than he can finish
practicalConstraints: Needs permission before sharing community recordings

biography.selfDescription: I notice sounds before I notice a lot of other things. I like asking people about a place, but being allowed to hear a story does not automatically mean I should put the whole thing in a video.
openQuestions: Would hotter, denser surroundings widen his interests or wear him down?
Does he enjoy analysis as much as field observation?

biography.name: Linh Cabrera

background.family: Lives with her adoptive parents and older adopted brother; both children have different birth-family contact arrangements that are discussed without comparison.
background.finances: Stable middle income from nursing and city employment; activity fees are manageable with planning.
background.geography: San Marcos, Texas, close to a river and a university campus.
background.cultureLanguages: Vietnamese American teenager in a Mexican American and white household; English predominates, with Spanish from relatives and beginner Vietnamese lessons by choice.
background.school: Public high school with outdoor education and art electives.
background.accessOpportunities: Has access to campus public events, river volunteers, and family-supported language tutoring.

timeline.story: Linh liked mixing paint and then trying to name the resulting colors. Her parents kept her sprawling pictures on a low wall, where she regularly changed their order to tell a new story.

She began weekend walks beside the river and asked why some banks had bare soil. A volunteer explained erosion using a handful of dirt, and Linh repeated the demonstration in the bathtub until cleanup rules were negotiated.

A school heritage project made her uncomfortable because classmates expected one simple family story. Her parents helped her present several relationships and unanswered questions, while letting her decide which private details belonged off the poster.

She learned to knit through video calls with an aunt during remote school. Counting stitches irritated her, but the repeated hand movement helped her listen to long conversations, and she made uneven but warmly received scarves.

Linh chose Vietnamese lessons after meeting another adopted teenager, then nearly quit when progress felt slow. Her teacher used songs and everyday phrases, making the lessons less like a test of whether she belonged.

River cleanups introduced her to collecting and classifying small debris. She created a collage from washed wrappers for art class, but resisted a teacher’s suggestion that every subsequent piece should carry an environmental message.

Now she combines outdoor volunteering, drawing, and occasional knitting while exploring university and community-college events nearby. She wants room to change her interests and her relationship to heritage without other people treating either as a solved assignment. A teacher’s enthusiastic interpretation of one drawing also taught her to say politely when an explanation did not match her intention.

avoids: Pressure to make every hobby meaningful
motivations: Freedom to revise her own story
ambitions: Wants more independent exploration
Imagines daily access to nature and a home where complicated family histories are ordinary.

biography.selfDescription: Sometimes a drawing is just colors I wanted to put together. I can care about the river and my family and where I came from without making every project explain all of it.
openQuestions: Will language lessons remain a personal choice over time?
Does she enjoy systematic field observation apart from volunteering?

biography.name: Owen Chao

background.family: Lives with parents and an older sister; they share cooking and often host relatives for game nights.
background.finances: Working-class household with stable rent and little accumulated savings; Owen’s part-time earnings are mostly his to save.
background.geography: El Paso, Texas, near a bus route and several public parks.
background.cultureLanguages: Chinese American father and Mexican American mother; English and Spanish are used daily, with Cantonese phrases from grandparents.
background.school: Public early-college high school; enjoys some dual-credit courses but finds its frequent future planning repetitive.
background.accessOpportunities: Public library, community chess, school labs, and regional college or technical programs offer practical routes.

timeline.story: Owen liked drawing floor plans for houses where every room had an implausible purpose, including a room just for turning around. Adults kept his drawings because his explanations were so much fun to hear.

His sister taught him chess, and he liked reconstructing games more than playing rapidly. He also spent afternoons kicking a ball against a wall, pleased by the different sounds different surfaces produced.

Helping prepare dumplings and tamales introduced him to repeated tasks with many acceptable variations. He became good at noticing when a batch needed more water, but disliked anyone turning family cooking into a competition.

During remote lessons he took photographs of shadows moving across the patio and compared them over several days. A teacher suggested a science fair, but Owen preferred keeping a casual notebook without making a presentation.

Early-college classes brought older classmates and more responsibility for deadlines. He struggled initially with asking professors questions, then found that writing a precise email was easier than waiting until confusion had become overwhelming.

He began cashier shifts at a neighborhood market and appreciated coworkers who taught small practical shortcuts. Chess remained social rather than competitive, and he started sketching small comics about customers without using recognizable identifying details.

Owen currently combines dual-credit study, market shifts, and family cooking. He is curious about many systems but resists having every observation turned into an application; he wants affordable education with room for ordinary pleasures and a schedule he can sustain.

ambitions: Wants affordable continued education
Imagines a modest home near good food, public spaces, and people he can see regularly.
struggles: Pressure to turn curiosity into credentials

biography.selfDescription: Sometimes I want to find out what happens without entering a competition about it. I'm not against having plans; I just want the plans to leave enough room for the things that make a normal Tuesday good.
openQuestions: Would a longer self-directed investigation appeal?
Does he dislike public presentation or the pressure attached to it?

biography.name: Amara Knox

background.family: Lives with parents and a younger sister; everyone has household tasks and negotiates who needs assistance with what.
background.finances: Middle income from legal support and equipment sales; accessibility costs influence housing and travel decisions.
background.geography: Georgetown, Texas, in an accessible single-story house.
background.cultureLanguages: Black American family with English at home and close relationships across several Texas cities.
background.school: Public high school; fictional cerebral palsy affects lower-body mobility, and she uses a wheelchair with an accessibility and transport plan.
background.accessOpportunities: Accessible school media spaces and family advocacy offer opportunities; some off-campus venues still require advance checking.

timeline.story: Amara loved sorting costume jewelry and announcing pretend auctions with extravagant descriptions. Her wheelchair was part of daily movement, while her family’s clearest memory from that period was how seriously she took imaginary bidding rules.

At school she enjoyed reading aloud and making classmates laugh with dramatic character voices. A playground redesign let her join more games, and she insisted on helping choose rules instead of only being assigned a spectator role.

She started photographing neighborhood details from angles adults overlooked. A relative gave her a small camera, and she discovered that an ordinary curb or window could look different when she waited for the right light.

During remote learning she made a family photo archive and interviewed relatives by phone. She liked their stories but learned to ask permission before sharing photographs, especially when someone’s favorite memory involved another person’s embarrassment.

Joining the school news team introduced caption editing and careful fact checking. She enjoyed preparing an interview more than being on camera, though classmates sometimes pushed her toward public inspiration stories she had never volunteered to tell.

Amara helped evaluate access for a school trip while another student handled the main itinerary. The trip went well, but she resented the extra planning labor and asked adults to make access checks a standard responsibility next time.

She edits school news, takes photographs, and attends occasional accessible recreation sessions. She is investigating Texas study options through actual routes and housing details, while keeping questions about courses and friendships equally central to her decisions.

ambitions: Wants further education and independent housing
Imagines a connected neighborhood where getting out to meet friends takes little negotiation.

biography.selfDescription: I like asking the questions more than being the interview subject. I want people to remember access before I arrive, so I can spend more time thinking about the same interesting things everyone else came for.
openQuestions: Would she enjoy reporting unfamiliar or contentious subjects?
Which environments distribute access work reliably?

biography.name: Rowan Yazzie

background.family: Lives with their mother and stepfather; spends part of each summer with relatives in northern New Mexico.
background.finances: Modest stable income from remote administrative work and utility maintenance.
background.geography: Las Cruces, New Mexico, with regular family trips toward El Paso.
background.cultureLanguages: Diné and Anglo family connections; English is their strongest language, with limited Diné Bizaad learned from relatives and conversational Spanish from neighbors.
background.school: Parent-directed home education using library courses, a math tutor, and loosely scheduled personal projects.
background.accessOpportunities: Community classes nearby and possible El Paso Community College or UTEP public programs; Texas options require checking travel costs and nonresident tuition.

timeline.story: Rowan liked tracing the shadows of porch posts and listening to relatives tell the same event differently. They resisted group craft instructions but could spend a long time copying a particular curve in a family photograph.

Home education began after a family move disrupted kindergarten. Their mother scheduled reading each morning but let afternoons follow questions, including several weeks spent making paper maps of imaginary irrigation channels.

They became fascinated by a neighbor's ham radio and less fascinated by memorizing the procedures needed to use it. A tutor introduced regular math practice, which Rowan initially resented and later appreciated when measurements became easier.

A library drama group gave them their first recurring peer activity. They loved rehearsing dialogue, found spontaneous games uncomfortable, and learned that asking for the day's outline made attendance much easier.

Rowan interviewed relatives for an audio project and realized that recording someone requires more than good questions. A cousin asked for a story to be removed; Rowan complied and revised their consent process for later interviews.

They tried a structured community science course and enjoyed the equipment, deadlines, and people more than expected. Keeping written lab notes was difficult because their private projects rarely required anyone else to follow the process.

They now combine a weekly science class with a small audio drama made by friends. They wonder whether a conventional classroom would offer welcome structure or too little choice, and are practicing meeting deadlines that someone else sets.

motivations: Having both freedom and reliable expectations
ambitions: Try a longer classroom course
Complete a shared audio episode on schedule
They imagine a home with quiet project space and regular chances to learn with other people, without knowing where it should be.
struggles: Some weeks lack enough peer contact
practicalConstraints: Need to document home education for applications

biography.selfDescription: I am used to having time to follow an interesting detour. I also like knowing exactly when other people expect something from me, which surprises people who hear that I learn at home.
openQuestions: How much externally set structure would they prefer?
Would regular peer contact matter more than subject choice?

biography.name: Grant Whitlock

background.family: Lives with his parents and older sister on acreage; family relationships are steady and disagreements are generally direct.
background.finances: Affluent household supported by a regional construction business and a salaried engineering job.
background.geography: Outside Weatherford, Texas, with a long drive to most organized activities.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking family whose gatherings combine country music, competitive card games, and discussions of local history.
background.school: Small private school using a classical curriculum; students give frequent oral presentations.
background.accessOpportunities: Weatherford College classes and Fort Worth museum programs are feasible with rides; parents can pay for equipment but cannot drive every day.

timeline.story: Grant liked digging channels after rain and announcing which puddle would drain first. He told visitors his predictions as facts, even when water quickly proved him wrong.

He learned to read early and spent long afternoons with illustrated history books. His parents introduced several sports; he liked wearing the uniform and disliked almost every practice, eventually keeping only recreational swimming.

He built a crude backyard weather station with his sister. She maintained the records after his interest shifted to making mock radio announcements, although he continued referring to the station as their shared scientific project.

School presentations became easy for him, and adults often described him as mature. An archaeological demonstration exposed a weakness: he wanted to tell the story before patiently recording what had actually been found.

He joined a history performance event, researching a little and improvising a lot. Feedback about unsupported details irritated him. Meanwhile, he began drawing careful floor plans for imaginary houses without showing anyone the dozens of revisions.

A theater teacher gave him a minor role and a demanding set-painting assignment. He enjoyed collaborating more than expected but lost track of cleanup duties. His sister asked him to stop promising help unless he wrote down the date.

Grant is enthusiastic about weather, buildings, and historical storytelling, with deeper practice in drawing than he usually admits. He talks confidently about future independence while still relying on family to manage much of his schedule and several unfinished projects.

ambitions: Finish and document one weather project
Imagine an adult home with space for friends and projects, though he has not thought through its upkeep
practicalConstraints: Limited experience managing money or appointments

biography.selfDescription: I am comfortable telling people what I think. The drawings in my room take longer than my presentations, and I sometimes wish people noticed that I do work at things quietly too.
openQuestions: Will responsibility for maintenance alter his attraction to large projects?
How does he handle evidence that changes an appealing story?

biography.name: Parisa Rahmani

background.family: Lives with her parents and three siblings; family life is busy but predictable, with cousins nearby and rotating responsibilities.
background.finances: Stable middle income from accounting and restaurant management.
background.geography: North Dallas, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Afghan American family established in Texas before she was born; English and Dari, with varied religious practice among relatives.
background.school: Public high school with wrestling, earth science, and media electives.
background.accessOpportunities: Dallas College events, city recreation, and university outreach are reachable; family schedules determine which evenings are practical.

timeline.story: Parisa liked telling dramatic stories to her siblings and arranging stones by imaginary market value. Her parents did not know which activity would last, and neither did she.

She joined a recreation gymnastics group and enjoyed strength exercises more than performing routines. At home she learned basic crochet, undoing mistakes with a patience she did not show when interrupted during a story.

A museum display made her curious about rocks that looked plain outside and different inside. She kept a small collection and wrote exaggerated labels, combining actual facts with a fictional voice until a teacher asked her to distinguish them.

She volunteered to narrate a class performance and loved the microphone. Group science work was harder because she sometimes took over explanations before others finished testing. A friend's direct complaint persuaded her to ask more questions.

Parisa tried wrestling at a school open session and enjoyed learning a movement she could not master immediately. She continued crochet during quiet evenings and began listening to interviews with athletes about practice rather than victories.

She joined wrestling and a media class, making a short interview piece about people who repair ordinary objects. Editing other people's words required restraint she found difficult. A geology field day reignited her interest in stones beyond collecting attractive ones.

She competes occasionally, crochets gifts, and studies earth science with growing interest. She likes public explanation but does not yet know whether she enjoys sustained investigation when there is no performance at the end. Her family encourages trying before announcing a lifelong plan.

avoids: Being treated as a spokesperson for all Afghan families
Unstructured projects where she cannot tell who is doing what
motivations: Telling an accurate and engaging story
ambitions: Complete an interview piece with fair shared credit
She imagines an adult life with a close community, physical activity, and evenings that can sometimes be completely quiet
struggles: May enjoy presenting more than investigating

biography.selfDescription: I like being heard, and I am working on hearing people all the way through. Repeating a wrestling move and repeating a crochet stitch feel more alike to me than people expect.
openQuestions: Will geology hold her interest through slow classification work?
How does she respond when someone else shapes the final story?

biography.name: Elena Castillo-Brooks

background.family: Lives with her mother, stepfather, and baby brother; adults did not attend college and openly ask questions alongside her.
background.finances: Stable lower middle income from skilled trades and office reception, with careful saving for future education.
background.geography: Pasadena, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Mexican American and white family connections; English at home with Spanish used frequently among extended relatives.
background.school: Academically structured public charter with frequent tests, clear homework routines, and limited workshop space.
background.accessOpportunities: San Jacinto College visits, public libraries, and Houston-area museum programs are feasible through school trips or family weekends.

timeline.story: Elena liked memorizing songs and asking adults to quiz her about picture books. She avoided messy painting at first, then happily used a wide brush when nobody expected a recognizable picture.

She enjoyed school rules and quickly learned what counted as a finished assignment. At home she helped measure rice and water, finding satisfaction in a repeatable result rather than inventing new dishes.

Her grandmother began teaching her more Spanish through stories. Elena understood much more than she would say aloud, worried about errors. She also loved a museum's oversized building blocks but assumed real construction was something other people understood.

Good grades became a reliable part of her identity. A loosely defined art assignment upset her because she could not tell what the teacher wanted. Her mother helped her submit a choice she liked rather than repeatedly asking for the hidden correct answer.

She joined a book club and discovered that disagreement could improve discussion without anyone losing points. A chemistry unit appealed through its explanations, though she had little chance to design an experiment herself.

At a public workshop, Elena built a small wooden tray with guidance. She measured accurately, made one repairable mistake, and kept calling the result luck. Caring for her baby brother also showed her that instructions do not cover every situation.

She remains academically successful and is trying a weekend cooking group where participants adapt recipes. She wants more experience making and testing things, but unfamiliar tasks expose how little she trusts competence that cannot be confirmed by a grade.

demonstratedSkills: Responding patiently to a baby's changing needs
motivations: Learning beyond getting the expected answer
Making education understandable to her family
ambitions: Try another practical workshop and keep the imperfect result
She imagines an adult life with stability, close family contact, and confidence to attempt unfamiliar things without constant reassurance

biography.selfDescription: I know how to be a good student, but I am still finding out how I learn when nobody gives me a model answer. The tray I made is on my desk, including the part I fixed.
openQuestions: How will she respond to sustained open-ended work with supportive feedback?
Will practical experience broaden or clarify her academic interests?

biography.name: Evan Liang

background.family: Lives with two parents and a younger sister; grandparents visit for several months most years.
background.finances: Stable middle income; the family budgets deliberately and rarely buys upgrades simply because something newer exists.
background.geography: A suburb north of Houston, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English is easiest for him; he uses limited Mandarin with grandparents and dislikes relatives testing his vocabulary.
background.school: Large public high school where he knows a small circle well and many classmates only by sight.
background.accessOpportunities: Has access to several clubs and reliable family transport, but parents prefer commitments that do not disrupt evenings.

timeline.story: Evan liked building cushions into a tunnel and changing the route after his sister crawled through it. He was quiet around unfamiliar adults and louder at home. At preschool he followed the craft instructions carefully, though he sometimes hid unfinished work because he disliked having it displayed.

He spent months learning a card game from his grandfather and enjoyed remembering which cards had already appeared. Losing could make him sullen. He also liked gardening that year, mainly digging small channels for water, and abandoned it when hot weather made the yard unpleasant after school.

During group projects Evan noticed which classmates wanted to draw and which wanted to present. He quietly offered trades so he could assemble the written parts. A teacher praised his contribution in front of the class, which embarrassed him enough that he avoided volunteering for the next project.

He joined an after-school games group and liked predicting what another player might accept in an exchange. He sometimes waited too long for a better offer and ended with nothing. At home he tried baking bread with his sister but disliked cleaning the sticky mixing bowl afterward.

Two school clubs wanted the same lunch meeting slot. Evan spoke individually with several members and discovered one group mainly wanted access to a particular room. He suggested alternating rooms instead of times. Someone else explained the arrangement publicly, and Evan was relieved to receive little attention.

In a strategy club he became the person who asked what each side would accept when rules or meeting plans were disputed. He preferred private conversations to arguing across a table. Sometimes his compromise avoided the real disagreement, and one friend accused him of caring more about peace than fairness.

Evan helped two clubs divide a shared supply cupboard by asking which materials each actually used. The arrangement worked for several weeks before unlabeled items reappeared. He is willing to revisit the agreement but reluctant to enforce it publicly. Outside school he enjoys cooking simple noodles and watching absurd comedy with his sister.

enjoys: Finding terms both groups can accept
avoids: Enforcing rules in a crowded room
unfamiliarActivities: Handling a dispute where compromise is impossible
ambitions: Have a room of his own someday
Become more comfortable disagreeing directly
Spend time somewhere his family has never visited
struggles: Sometimes treats quiet as proof a disagreement is resolved
supports: A sister who challenges his evasions
A club advisor who lets him prepare before speaking
practicalConstraints: Does not want every interest to become a commitment

biography.selfDescription: I like figuring out what people would actually agree to. Being the person at the microphone sounds exhausting.
openQuestions: When is he willing to risk an openly unhappy response?
Does he enjoy negotiation when relationships do not become calmer afterward?

biography.name: Jordan Fuentes

background.family: Lives with their mother and mother’s partner; sees their father some weekends, with changing arrangements.
background.finances: Bills are usually covered, but replacing broken devices takes negotiation and saving.
background.geography: San Antonio apartment complex near a busy arterial road.
background.cultureLanguages: English and conversational Spanish; different relatives use different names and pronouns for them.
background.school: Large public school with an introductory computing class and a crowded device checkout program.
background.accessOpportunities: Uses a refurbished laptop; an older cousin shares explanations by voice message, but home support varies.

timeline.story: Jordan liked pressing the same button on a toy cash register until they understood which drawer movement followed it. They also made elaborate blanket forts with cousins. Their mother remembers constant questions; Jordan remembers mostly wanting adults to stop answering questions they had not asked.

They discovered that changing a saved game name did not change the name displayed everywhere. An uncle explained that separate places could store separate copies. Jordan forgot most of his explanation but remembered the annoyance, and began looking for other things that updated in one place but not another.

A school activity used colored blocks to move a character. Jordan made the character repeat a short path, then spent a whole session fixing an unwanted extra turn. They did not want to draw a background, although classmates were much more interested in adding costumes and music.

They made a tiny list for tracking borrowed books on an old tablet, then lost the file during a reset. Jordan was upset less about the appearance than about the unanswered question of why the saving step failed. Their cousin helped recover one earlier copy, but several entries remained missing.

A clinician described Jordan’s prolonged low mood, sleep disruption, and withdrawal as depression. Their mother arranged appointments when shifts allowed; their father called it too much screen time. Some weeks Jordan still enjoyed debugging small programs, and some weeks even opening the laptop felt like an unreasonable task.

In computing class they made a reminder script that sent duplicate alerts until they found a loop running twice. They liked isolating the error and disliked presenting the result with a sales-style introduction. An unfinished attendance utility stayed unfinished after a difficult month; praise did not automatically restore their momentum.

Jordan currently maintains a small household list that synchronizes when the connection returns. They enjoy making ordinary digital pieces cooperate, but resist relatives who demand a grand ambition from that fact. Appointments and support remain uneven, and they are unsure which household promises they can consistently keep.

enjoys: Tracing why a small program behaves unexpectedly
Making lists and reminders work reliably
Watching quiet comedy with their cousin
avoids: Being given responsibility without an agreed limit
activities: Helps a neighbor with simple device settings for occasional pay
ambitions: Keep one small system working for a full term
Have enough steadiness to choose their own next commitment
practicalConstraints: Uncertain time and energy for added duties

biography.selfDescription: “The button should do the thing it says. Getting that right is satisfying. Please do not make me sell the button.”
openQuestions: What responsibility can they sustain across uneven weeks?
Would they enjoy collaborative technical work with clear boundaries?
Which current supports will remain available next term?

biography.name: Elena Ríos

background.family: Lives with her mother, grandmother, and younger brother; her father visits on irregular weekends.
background.finances: Bills usually get paid, but replacement electronics and school trips require saving.
background.geography: An older apartment complex in Garland, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Uses Spanish with her grandmother and English at school; dislikes being asked to represent either culture.
background.school: Large public high school with crowded classes and a quiet resource room she can use.
background.accessOpportunities: Library internet, a borrowed tablet, and occasional rides from her aunt; few paid activities.

timeline.story: Elena lined up her plastic animals beside the bathtub, then became annoyed when her brother changed the order. She liked telling her grandmother which animals lived in water. She could repeat explanations from television without understanding all their words and sometimes argued when corrected.

Her mother remembers elaborate explanations of card game rules that nobody had requested. Elena liked demonstrating a rule with actual cards but hated deciding who went first. At school she enjoyed picture books about weather and avoided noisy birthday games, even when her friends participated.

After an autism diagnosis, adults discussed accommodations around her more often than she liked. A teacher let her prepare before speaking. Elena explained a rain experiment to a classmate three different ways, then cried when asked to lead the entire table through cleanup.

During remote lessons she made little diagrams for her brother when his fraction homework confused him. Some diagrams were wrong, and she erased them reluctantly after her mother checked. She also spent afternoons watching silly pet videos and left several science kits untouched beneath her bed.

A friend said Elena made everything sound like a lecture. She began asking what part was confusing before drawing examples, although she sometimes forgot to wait for an answer. She liked a small lunch group but declined arranging its movie outing because collecting everyone’s preferences felt exhausting.

She voluntarily helped two classmates understand density by comparing containers from home. When one example failed, she asked the teacher and rewrote it. Her group project went badly when everyone assumed she would allocate tasks. She enjoyed designing the explanation and resented tracking missing contributions.

Elena now shares short annotated examples in a class chat when someone requests help. She likes seeing the point at which another person understands, but repeated interruptions can make her abrupt. She still needs reminders about assignments and has not tried explaining anything regularly to unfamiliar younger children.

enjoys: Finding a second example when the first explanation fails
Subtitled comedy clips with her brother
avoids: Being volunteered to speak without preparation
activities: Shares homework examples with two friends
demonstratedSkills: Revises examples after checking an error
Remembers details from material she likes
motivations: Wants another person to understand without feeling foolish
ambitions: Make an explanation booklet that her brother actually uses
Try one optional advanced science class
struggles: Assuming her favorite example is obvious
supports: A teacher who answers follow-up questions
practicalConstraints: Unpredictable visits can change weekend plans

biography.selfDescription: I can explain something well after I have messed up the explanation once. People think that means I want to be in charge, but I do not. I also talk too much sometimes and miss what somebody actually asked.
openQuestions: Would explaining unfamiliar material still be enjoyable?
How much preparation does she need with new people?
Which parts of science interest her beyond helping classmates?

biography.name: Diego Moreno

background.family: Lives with his father, stepmother, and two younger siblings; his mother lives nearby.
background.finances: Stable modest income; small supplies are possible if planned.
background.geography: El Paso, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Spanish and English across both homes; relatives regularly cross between different family traditions.
background.school: Neighborhood public high school with several clubs he has chosen not to join.
background.accessOpportunities: Public library, a basic phone camera, family rides when arranged, and inexpensive paper supplies.

timeline.story: Diego liked folding paper into small houses and placing a toy animal inside. He resisted joining cousins in loud chase games, sometimes sitting beside his mother instead. Adults remember him as stubborn, but he did enjoy a calm game of hiding objects when nobody made it a competition.

A classroom animation using cutout shapes caught his attention. At home he moved a paper dog across a table while his father took pictures. He disliked being filmed himself. His first sequence barely moved when played back, and he abandoned it until his father showed him how to take more photographs.

He made another paper sequence about a hat blowing away, using a borrowed tablet. His cousins offered to provide voices, but he preferred silent motion and declined. He tried a team sport for several weeks, disliked practices and games, and was relieved when his parents accepted that answer.

Remote school left him making tiny stop-motion clips beside the kitchen window. Some clips were only six seconds long. He liked changing the spacing between frames and did not like writing stories about the characters. He also avoided online multiplayer games because the constant conversation and competition annoyed him.

A teacher suggested drama, drawing club, and a group video activity after seeing one clip. Diego tried drawing club twice and disliked the shared prompts. He declined drama outright. He kept making short paper movements at home, even though adults worried that his narrow choices meant he was missing something.

He spent a month making a folded bird turn its head convincingly. Several versions looked worse than the first, and he left the materials untouched for days. A friend wanted a longer funny film together. Diego refused because planning dialogue and negotiating scenes sounded unpleasant, though the refusal strained their friendship.

Diego makes brief silent paper animations when he wants to, sometimes once a week and sometimes less. He dislikes sports, public performing, persuasion, group planning, and most assigned creative prompts from actual experience. He does not want to choose an alternative merely to seem agreeable, but admits he has barely tried many solitary activities.

enjoys: Changing frame spacing in very short paper animations
Walking familiar routes alone in daylight
activities: Watches a few animation process videos
demonstratedSkills: Notices small differences in movement between frames
Repeats a short sequence to improve timing
States a preference clearly even when others disagree
unfamiliarActivities: Making a project for someone else’s specifications
motivations: Likes controlling a tiny movement until it looks right
Wants adults to accept a sincere refusal
ambitions: Make a paper bird land without its wing wobbling
Keep a folder of clips he likes
struggles: Avoids discussing why he dislikes something
Stops working when revisions become irritating
supports: Father who lends a phone stand
Mother who keeps a supply envelope for him
One friend who watches clips without requesting a bigger project
practicalConstraints: Phone needed by family at times
Limited storage for fragile paper pieces

biography.selfDescription: I have tried some of the things people keep suggesting, and I did not like them. Making a paper thing move is different. I am not saying I know every possible thing I like, but I am not going to say I want a club just to end the conversation.
openQuestions: Which unfamiliar solitary activities would he willingly try?
How much of the animation process remains appealing under external requirements?
Can he express refusals while maintaining friendships?
